question: What part of a red blood cell decides a person's blood group?
explanation: Think of surface antigens like name tags on the outside of red blood cells. They tell the body which blood group the cells belong to! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: In Nigerian hospitals, why do we always check the ABO and Rhesus blood systems first?

options.A: They change frequently based on diet and environmental factors
options.B: They trigger the most severe and common transfusion reactions
options.C: They require no laboratory equipment to test accurately
options.D: They are the only blood groups present in human blood

explanation: Getting these two wrong during a blood transfusion can cause very dangerous reactions, which is why nurses check them carefully every single time. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: If a patient has blood group A, which natural antibodies do they have floating in their plasma?
explanation: The body is smart! It naturally makes antibodies against whatever blood antigen it *doesn't* have on its own cells. So group A cells carry anti-B antibodies. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why is someone with blood group AB called a 'universal recipient' for red blood cells?

options.A: Their plasma contains no antibodies to attack incoming donor red blood cells
options.B: Their bone marrow rapidly destroys any mismatched red blood cells
options.C: Their immune system is permanently suppressed against foreign proteins
options.D: Their red blood cells lack all surface antigens that could trigger a reaction

explanation: Group AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies lying in wait, meaning it won't fight off incoming donor red blood cells! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: How is the Rhesus (Rh) antibody response different from the ABO antibody response?

options.A: Rh antibodies only develop after exposure to foreign Rh antigens
options.B: Rh antibodies completely disappear within a few weeks of exposure
options.C: Rh antibodies are passed directly through casual skin contact
options.D: Rh antibodies are present in everyone at birth regardless of type

explanation: Unlike ABO antibodies that you are born with, your body only builds Rh antibodies if an Rh-negative person is actually exposed to Rh-positive blood first. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: An Rh-negative patient gets an accidental transfusion of Rh-positive blood for the very first time. What happens inside their body?

options.A: Primary sensitization occurs, with gradual antibody production over weeks
options.B: Instant anaphylactic shock occurs due to pre-existing anti-D antibodies
options.C: Immediate massive hemolysis destroys all transfused red blood cells
options.D: No immune response occurs because Rh-negative blood has no antigens

explanation: Since it's their first exposure, there's no immediate explosion—instead, the immune system slowly wakes up and starts building antibodies over the following weeks. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: During a lab crossmatch, what visual result tells you that the donor and patient blood are incompatible?
explanation: Agglutination simply means clumping! If the red blood cells clump together in the test tube, it's a red flag that the blood types don't match. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why do medical lab scientists use both forward and reverse typing for ABO blood groups?

options.A: To identify hidden infections transmitted through donor blood
options.B: To measure the exact hemoglobin concentration in plasma
options.C: To determine if the patient has a Rhesus negative status
options.D: To cross-check results and prevent fatal typing errors

explanation: Doing two different tests acts like a double-check system to make sure no dangerous mistakes slip through before a patient gets blood. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which blood group is the universal donor for packed red blood cells?
explanation: Group O red blood cells don't have A or B antigens on them, so practically any patient's immune system can accept them without attacking! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why do the rules for giving donated plasma work in reverse compared to giving red blood cells?

options.A: Plasma contains high concentrations of hemoglobin that alter the recipient blood group
options.B: Plasma antibodies change their type immediately upon contact with recipient veins
options.C: Donor red blood cells destroy plasma proteins before they enter the general circulation
options.D: Plasma transfusions introduce donor antibodies that can attack recipient red blood cells

explanation: When giving plasma, you have to worry about the antibodies floating in the donor's liquid part fighting the patient's cells! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is a major, dangerous complication of an acute mismatched blood transfusion?
explanation: When mismatched blood cells burst open, all the loose hemoglobin floods the kidneys and can quickly clog them up, leading to kidney injury. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)

question: Why is Rho(D) immune globulin given to an Rh-negative mother after childbirth?

options.A: To permanently convert the mother's blood group to Rh-positive
options.B: To stimulate the foetus to produce its own protective antibodies
options.C: To cure existing hemolytic disease in the unborn foetus
options.D: To prevent maternal sensitization against foetal Rh-positive red blood cells

explanation: It acts like a cleanup crew, destroying any baby blood cells that slipped into the mother's system before her body can spot them and build lifelong antibodies. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)
